costGuide.labourLine: Fitting a Mercedes M278.990 typically takes 16-22 hours at £65/hr (independent specialist rate) - confirm exact labour when comparing quotes, as the hot-vee turbo layout and 4MATIC integration significantly increase labour time.
paragraphs: The final cost of a Mercedes M278.990 engine replacement is heavily influenced by whether the unit requires cylinder bore sleeving to address lining scuffing, and the condition of the twin turbochargers. If turbo failure has caused internal oil contamination or if the cylinder walls are severely scored, a standard reconditioned swap may not suffice, pushing the requirement toward a fully rebuilt unit with upgraded thermal management components. failures.title: Mercedes M278.990 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Cylinder Lining Scuffing (Nikasil Coating Wear)
items.whatHappens: Early production M278 engines are susceptible to cylinder wall scoring and Nikasil coating degradation. This manifests as excessive oil consumption, blue smoke from the exhaust, misfires, and a progressive loss of compression. If ignored, the scoring worsens, leading to catastrophic bottom-end damage from oil starvation.
items.repairVsReplace: If caught early, the block can sometimes be sleeved or line-bored, but the labour intensity and risk of underlying damage often make a full Mercedes M278.990 engine replacement the more reliable long-term solution.

items.title: Timing Chain Stretch and Guide Wear
items.whatHappens: Sharing the hot-vee V8 architecture with the M273 and M157, the M278 is prone to timing chain stretch and plastic guide wear over time. This manifests as a distinct metallic rattling noise on cold starts, followed by check engine lights indicating camshaft correlation faults. If ignored, the chain can jump teeth, leading to catastrophic valve-to-piston contact.
items.repairVsReplace: If caught early, replacing the timing chain kit, tensioners, and guides is viable, though it is a highly labour-intensive job requiring significant front-end strip-down. If internal damage has already occurred, a full Mercedes M278.990 engine replacement is the only reliable solution.

items.title: Turbocharger Wastegate Rattle and Valley Pan Oil Leaks
items.whatHappens: The hot-vee layout places the twin turbochargers directly in the valley between the cylinder banks, subjecting them to extreme heat. This accelerates wastegate actuator wear and linkage rattle, leading to boost pressure faults. Additionally, the heat cycles cause the valley pan seals and oil cooler O-rings to harden and crack, resulting in persistent oil leaks and a burning oil smell in the cabin.
items.repairVsReplace: Wastegate actuators and valley pan seals can be replaced as preventative maintenance. However, if turbo bearing wear has led to oil ingestion and internal engine scoring, a full rebuild is necessary to prevent repeat failure.

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the Mercedes M278.990
variants.intro: The M278.990 engine code is stamped directly onto a machined pad on the engine block, typically located near the oil filter housing or the bell housing. It is also clearly listed on your vehicle's V5C registration document under "Engine Number" and can be decoded from the full VIN. Common Confusion Warning: Owners frequently confuse the M278.990 with other Mercedes V8 engines: - M278.920/940/950/960: The standard 4.6L and 5.5L variants of this engine family. While mechanically similar, the .990 is the specific high-output 5.5L 4MATIC variant with different ECU mapping, exhaust routing, and 4MATIC integration. Fitting a lower-output variant will result in ECU and drivetrain incompatibilities. - M157: The AMG-specific 5.5L biturbo V8. While sharing similar displacement, the M157 features AMG-specific engine mounts, ECU calibration, and exhaust routing, making it incompatible as a direct swap for a standard M278.990. - M177: The newer 4.0L AMG biturbo V8. It features a completely different block architecture, hot-vee turbo sizing, and engine management system. Fitting the wrong revision will result in severe ECU, wiring loom, and exhaust manifold incompatibilities.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement Mercedes M278.990 - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used Mercedes M278.990 is only advisable for lower-mileage host vehicles and *only* if accompanied by documented, stamped service history proving rigorous oil changes (every 5,000-8,000 miles) and no prior complaints of excessive oil consumption or cold-start rattles. The risk of inheriting cylinder lining scuffing or timing chain stretch is unacceptably high without this proof.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: This is the most recommended route for the M278.990. A proper reconditioned unit will include verified cylinder bore integrity (or sleeved bores if applicable), brand-new timing chain components, refreshed valley pan seals, and tested twin turbochargers, directly addressing the V8's known weak points out of the box.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full rebuild is justified if your original M278.990 suffered catastrophic cylinder scoring that damaged the pistons, or if severe turbo failure caused oil starvation to the crankshaft bearings. A specialist rebuild will machine the block, fit upgraded thermal management components, and ensure all oil galleries are clear.

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: Sourcing a replacement is only half the job. Our network provides full supply and fit services, ensuring the engine is installed by Mercedes and V8-specialist technicians with a nationwide warranty backing both the labour and the unit.
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: For flagship hosts like the W222 S-Class, X166 GLS, and X222 Maybach, current UK market values typically sit between £15,000 and £60,000 . With a reconditioned M278.990 replacement costing from £8,000 (plus £1,040-£1,430 fitting), the repair cost generally represents 20-40% of the vehicle's value, making replacement financially viable for well-maintained examples. However, for early W222 or X166 hosts valued under £12,000, we strongly advise evaluating the car's scrap or part-exchange value before committing to a V8 engine replacement.

items.question: What is the most common failure with the Mercedes M278.990 engine?
items.answer: The most documented failure patterns for the M278.990 are cylinder lining scuffing (Nikasil coating wear) and timing chain stretch. Early warning signs include excessive oil consumption, blue smoke, misfires, or a metallic rattle on cold starts, and if ignored, cylinder scoring worsens or the chain jumps teeth, leading to catastrophic valve-to-piston contact requiring full engine replacement.

items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned Mercedes M278.990 engine?
items.answer: A reconditioned Mercedes M278.990 is strongly recommended over a used unit due to the well-documented cylinder lining scuffing and timing chain failure risks. Used units carry a high probability of inheriting the same latent wear unless accompanied by stamped proof of preventative maintenance and no oil consumption complaints, whereas a proper reconditioned M278.990 includes verified cylinder bore integrity, new timing chain components, refreshed valley pan seals, and tested twin turbochargers as standard.

items.question: What is the difference between the M278.990 and other M278 or M157 variants?
items.answer: The M278.990 is the specific high-output 5.5L 4MATIC variant tuned for flagship sedans and SUVs. The standard M278 variants are typically rear-wheel-drive or have different ECU mapping, and the M157 is the AMG-specific variant with different mounts, ECU calibration, and exhaust routing, meaning fitting the wrong variant will result in severe mounting, wiring loom, and exhaust manifold incompatibilities.
